headline: Placed in the sin bin after three consecutive disappointments; retaining holding but unwilling to pay for earnings that have yet to arrive; material upside if Middle East conflicts resolve
reasoning: Worley has disappointed investors three times in quick succession — restructuring charges at the February result, a larger-than-expected Middle East and currency impact, and a weaker-than-anticipated FY27 outlook. Earnings quality is increasingly difficult to assess because underlying EBITA excludes approximately $120m of recurring restructuring costs, and procurement revenue (which grew ~35% at the first half) inflates reported turnover while contributing little incremental margin. Sustainability-related revenue has risen from one-third to nearly 70% of group revenue, yet FY26 group revenue was flat and underlying EBITA declined, breaking the expected nexus between sustainability exposure and shareholder value. The move into Full Project Delivery (EPC/EPCM) expands addressable spend but changes the risk profile by introducing execution complexity, lower margins and potential customer concentration. The firm will hold but is unwilling to capitalise earnings guided to arrive in six to twelve months; prices above approximately $13 are flagged as a likely reduction point. A resolution of Middle East conflicts is identified as the most material near-term upside catalyst.
quote: Worley is now in the sin bin. The FY27 outlook compounds our caution. Management expects growth, but earnings are again expected to be weighted towards the second half. After three disappointments in relatively quick succession, we are no longer prepared to capitalise earnings that management says will arrive in six or twelve months. For the next twelve months, Worley is effectively in our and the market's sin bin. This is not because we no longer believe in the underlying franchise. Rather, we have become tired of an attractive strategic story repeatedly being accompanied by earnings that arrive later, are lower than initially expected, or require another explanation. Chris Ashton and his team now need to demonstrate that the promised improvement is real. The next results need to contain more delivery and less promise.

headline: Clearbridge sees Worley's backlog rebuilding with LNG, data centres and energy resilience driving re-acceleration in growth
reasoning: Rhys Bertels notes Worley has had a tough 12–18 months after Trump's election caused cancellation of energy transition and green projects in the US. However, the pipeline is rebuilding through CP2, LNG projects, and energy infrastructure demand from data centres. Post the Iran war, he expects countries globally to build more energy resilience (fuel storage, etc.), which Worley will participate in. Worley has also undergone a cost reset through a shift to a central hub model. Additionally, AI is seen as a margin tailwind — Worley can use AI over its internal engineering knowledge base to make engineers more efficient, boosting margins without necessarily altering revenues.
quote: Warley's had a tough 12, 18 months. They'd been doing really well on sort of energy transition type projects and green projects, and with Trump coming in, a lot of those projects were cancelled. But they have been rebuilding the pipeline with CP2 and LNG, and also energy infrastructure demand, be it for data centres or the like, the need is growing strongly. So we clearly see the backlog rebuilding, and coming out of the Iran war, you're going to see countries everywhere build more in terms of their energy resilience and be it in Australia of building more diesel or fuel supply storage, Warley's going to be involved in those sorts of projects or involved in building data centres and design. They've gone through a cost reset through this period, moving a lot to a central hub. And we do think this is one of the companies that AI can be an advantage for, because it's not like people are going to start building complex LNG facilities using AI, but Warley using AI over its internal knowledge of its engineering programs can make its engineers far more efficient in delivering a product to customers. quote: WorleyParsons (WOR) fell -24.7% in the month. Late in the month, WOR announced a very material acquisition, where it purchased the Engineering, Chemicals and Resources divisions of US based competitor, Jacobs Engineering Group. The purchase price was $4.6B, which was essentially the same as WOR's market capitalisation at the time of the announcement. The acquisition was funded from a $2.95B equity raising, $1.0B of WOR stock issued to Jacobs and $0.9B of additional debt. Whilst there are clear positives of the acquisition in terms of potential cost synergies and earnings accretion, the short-term negative for the WOR stock price was the very large equity raising that was launched at a time where equity markets globally were being sold off heavily. In addition, there is quite significant integration risk given both businesses are people based and it will take some time to prove that the integration has been successful.
